newsitem.title: ITALY: Fiat future seen tough as 1996 disappoints.
newsitem.headline: Fiat future seen tough as 1996 disappoints.

text.p: Investors in Italian stocks took a dim view of carmaker Fiat on Friday following weak results in 1996 and analysts said the group had a tough time ahead in 1997 despite government incentives to make consumers buy cars.

Few analysts had altered recommendations on the stock so far after preliminary 1996 results were published on Thursday, saying they wanted to speak to the company before making changes. But some had lowered their profit forecasts.

"Out into 1997, Fiat has a tougher time ahead of it because of the relative strength of the lira which has handed some competitive advantage back to Volkswagen, Ford and General Motors," one London-based analyst said.
The share, which climbed in recent weeks with a general rally on the Italian stock market, was down 0.19 percent at 5,140 lire ($3.19) by 1520 GMT, after falling to a low of 4,980.

Fiat said in a letter to shareholders on Thursday its 1996 operating profits slid to around 1.8 trillion lire from 1995's 3.325 trillion, while annual sales rose just three percent to around 78 trillion lire.

Its 1996 pretax profit was provisionally 3.5 trillion lire from 3.404 trillion in 1995 after one-off gains from the flotation of 31 percent of agricultural machines maker New Holland on the New York stock market and a capital gain from the sale of its Prime fund management arm.

But its operating profit margin was squeezed to 2.3 percent from 4.4 percent in 1995. Christopher Will, European auto analyst at Lehman in London, said the fourth quarter operating margin was about 0.5 percent against 4.1 percent a year earlier.
"That's worrying because New Holland had a good quarter and Fiat Auto in Brazil had a good profitable quarter. This implies Fiat Auto in Europe is seeing a growth in losses."
Will cut his 1996 earnings per share forecast, before exceptionals, to 240 lire from 275, 1997 to 300 from 348 and 1998 to 310 from 387.
His recommendation was neutral but he added: "For the international investor, the stock has gone up 20 percent in January even if that's due to the Italian equity market.
"I would expect to see selling from international shareholders because these numbers were disappointing."

Banca Commerciale Italiana cut its 1997 net profit forecast to 1.5 trillion lire from 1.7 trillion but kept a recommendation to "reduce" above 5,000 lire per share with a target of 4,700, while Imi Sigeco revised down its 1996 net profit forecast.
Analysts saw a government incentive scheme this year to get consumers to scrap old cars for new as a double edged sword.

"The incentives are like having a big party and then a whopping hangover -- you get all the orders compressed into a short space of time and there's a drought the following year," said one London-based analyst who declined to be named.
Fiat said orders have risen around 35 percent in Italy in January as a result of the incentives.
But Will noted when France used incentives to stimulate its market, European carmakers in general took advantage of the scheme with aggressively low pricing on low end cars.

Last year Fiat was protected in the Italian market by the weak lira which made it difficult for other producers to sell in Italy profitably. But the lira's rise "means French and German producers can sell cars profitably in Italy and cut prices."
Others held recommendations steady before meeting the group.

Giuliana Porta at Albertini Sim, said the 1996 figures were weaker than forecast but added: "We're still evaluating them. The first impression is to maintain a positive valuation in the medium term, ignoring short term market weakness."
--Milan bureau +392 66129507 ($ = 1608 Italian Lire)
